The authenticated handler visibly checks its nonce and manage_options before reading input. It decodes and recursively applies sanitize_text_field in one statement. Core, content, plugin and MU locations are defined once as SSPA constants in the main plugin. WordPress has no location API for the database drop-in and MU installation directories; those helpers follow Query Monitor QM_Activation::activate/deactivate (classes/Activation.php): WP_CONTENT_DIR/db.php, DISALLOW_FILE_MODS, install only when absent, and remove only the owned helper with the network lifecycle guard. This is an owned database-helper precedent, not a precedent for replacing foreign files or writing data into mu-plugins. Standalone early profiling/observer code runs before the main plugin constants exist, and uninstall runs after deactivation, so those independent entry points read the WordPress locations directly. They never write into the plugin directory.

This is recovery only for a db.php or object-cache.php hold created by a version before 0.43.4. It restores the original file only if the destination is absent, preserves foreign files and dangling symlinks, and creates no new hold. Local rename preserves foreign symlinks and atomic ownership restoration; a filesystem copy/delete would change those semantics.

WordPress owns timestart; the profiler reads the core request-start timestamp to measure elapsed bootstrap time, without assigning it.

Super Speedy Filters owns ssf_archive_gate_policy and ssf_archive_gate_decision. The traffic observer reads the installed policy and calls the owner’s pure decision function to classify protection; it neither recreates nor writes that policy. Introducing a Filters-owned filter requires a separate change in that plugin.

The bundled Apache ECharts 6.1.0 custom build has a provenance/licence banner, linked legal notices, ECharts/zrender/d3 licence files and the ECharts NOTICE. Its readable entry point, exact dependency lock and build script are public in https://github.com/superspeedyplugins/super-speedy-performance-analysis/tree/main/.build/echarts ; the readme links the upstream source and reproducible npm ci / npm run build instructions. No chart code is fetched at runtime.

The signed-request profiler observes PHP warnings/notices as measurement evidence. Its handler returns false to preserve PHP’s normal error handling, chains/restores the previous handler, and is not installed for ordinary visitor requests.

Component and query attribution is the profiler’s purpose. The bounded backtrace identifies the plugin/theme responsible for measured work; it is not printed or logged as debug output. Capture/export privacy filters remove paths and argument values.

This read observes the existing third-party request solely to classify its transport or endpoint. It neither invokes the endpoint nor changes its authorisation or request fields. Scalars are unslashed and sanitised, endpoint identities are strictly allowlisted and validated, and only bounded local diagnostic evidence is recorded. Adding this plugin’s nonce to the observed request would change the workload being measured.

These are unauthenticated loopback measurements authorised by an expiring, path-bound HMAC and a database-backed single-use token. A cookie-user nonce cannot authorise them. The copied early-boot helper rejects non-string tokens and any byte outside its explicit character class, rejects control/space bytes in the request path, then verifies the exact signed bytes before arming capture. This runs before WordPress sanitisation and magic quoting; unslashing would alter signed input. The scanner does not recognise the prefixed sanitising functions.

Local rename preserves foreign symlinks and atomic ownership restoration; a filesystem copy/delete would change those semantics.

Performance Analysis captures and analyses mutable profiling evidence, coordinates single-use tokens and lifecycle leases, and owns its diagnostic tables. These reads and writes must observe the actual database state rather than a cached measurement. Application statements are prepared at their real call sites; the separately documented EXPLAIN and profiling-wpdb executors preserve captured SQL.

Meta-key/value reads identify plugin-owned temporary objects, measured order data and archive/query evidence using core APIs or the reviewed statements. Some matches are SQL text being inspected rather than an executed meta query. These heuristics do not indicate unbound input; caching mutable evidence would hide the change being measured.

This is the zero-argument read of the current PHP engine error mask, not a change to error reporting. The real signed-request case 66 proves ini_get returns the configured mask while @ suppression is active, incorrectly retaining suppressed warnings and turning a measured zero into one. Reading error_reporting() preserves suppression and normal PHP handling; the plugin never supplies an argument or changes the mask.

retained_sql_statements.S22: EXPLAIN describes the complete captured single eligible SELECT. Binding it as %s or %i explains a value or an identifier, not the captured query. The independent SHOW INDEX statement binds its table through %i and restricts it to current-database/current-prefix tables.
retained_sql_statements.S52: The multi-row Traffic INSERT binds its table through %i. Variable row counts and per-cell NULL layout require generated fragments containing fixed column names, placeholders and literal NULL, with every non-NULL value bound. WordPress value placeholders coerce NULL. Splitting the batch changes atomicity, failure behaviour, auto-increment allocation, trigger boundaries and round trips, so the approved single statement is retained unchanged.
